playground.label: Dictionaries: counting, grouping and merging (uses input)
playground.inputs: the cat and the hat and the bat

findings: Chapter 7 of the 3rd edition, Dictionaries and Structuring Data, teaches the dictionary data type as a mutable collection of key-value pairs between curly brackets, the KeyError of a missing key, the comparison of dictionaries with lists, the birthdays program, the methods keys(), values() and items() with in, not in and list(), the get() method, the setdefault() method with the characterCount program, the modelling of a chessboard as a dictionary with the Interactive Chessboard Simulator, nested dictionaries and lists with the guest picnic program, and closes with 8 practice questions and 3 practice programs.

The chapter's printed outputs reproduce under Python 3.14.4: KeyError: 0 and KeyError: 'color' and KeyError: 'eggs', the dict_keys, dict_values and dict_items forms, the exchange of the birthdays program, the count of characterCount with the same keys in the same order and the same numbers, and the five lines of guestpicnic, while the chessboard program runs and prints a text board (its Figure 7-3 is an image and was not compared), so that no printed output of the chapter differs; the differences lie in three statements of its prose and in its practice programs, given in the next findings.

The chapter says that items in dictionaries are unordered, that there is no first item, and that a dictionary is not a sequence because it is not ordered; since Python 3.7 a dictionary preserves insertion order as a language guarantee, where CPython 3.6 had it as an implementation detail, so that loops, list(d), keys(), values(), items() and popitem() follow it, replacing a value keeps the position of its key, and a key added after a deletion goes to the end; equality of dictionaries still ignores the order, and a dictionary is still not a sequence because its keys are not positions and it cannot be sliced.

The chapter says that a list or a dictionary cannot be a key because these types are unhashable, a concept it leaves out of the book; the data model defines the rule: a key must have a hash that does not change, objects that compare equal must have the same hash, a class that defines __eq__ without __hash__ is unhashable, and a tuple is a key only if everything in it is hashable; the consequences the chapter does not show are that 1, 1.0 and True are one key, that a tuple holding a list is refused, and that slice objects have been hashable since Python 3.12, so that d[0:2] is a KeyError and no longer a TypeError.

The chapter calls the results of keys(), values() and items() list-like values that cannot be modified; the documentation calls them view objects that show later changes of the dictionary, that are reversible since Python 3.8, that support the set operators for keys and items, and whose values view is never equal to another; the same documentation states that adding or deleting keys while iterating may raise RuntimeError, and it presents get(), setdefault(), collections.Counter and collections.defaultdict as the tools for absent keys, of which only a subscript calls the __missing__ method that defaultdict uses.

The chapter's text and practice programs are not consistent with its own notation: the text says the chessboard loops go from right to left while the code visits a to h, which is left to right; question 8 asks for the module and function that pretty-print dictionaries although the chapter as read does not teach pprint, which prints with sorted keys in pprint.pprint and in insertion order in pprint.pp; the Chess Dictionary Validator speaks of squares from '1a' to '8h' and of pieces named 'pawn' and 'knight' where the chapter's board uses 'a1' to 'h8' and 'wP' and 'bN'; and the sample outputs of the inventory programs list 12 arrow first and ruby before dagger, which is not the insertion order that a loop over items() follows for the dictionaries given.

For an advanced course, chapter 7 is best taught by asking of each dictionary operation whether it reads, adds or replaces, removes, or only looks, and what it does for a missing key: d[k] raises KeyError, get() and in do not, setdefault() and defaultdict add, pop() and del remove; the chapter's printed outputs all hold under 3.14.4, its statement that dictionaries are unordered must be replaced by insertion order, its hashing rule by the data model's, and what it leaves for the course to add are pop(), update(), the merge operators, comprehensions, Counter and defaultdict, the RuntimeError of changing a dictionary while looping, shallow and deep copies of nested data, TypedDict and mapping patterns.

Current Python gives dictionaries more than the chapter presents: pop(), popitem(), update(), clear(), copy() and fromkeys(), the dictionary comprehension (PEP 274, Python 2.7 and 3.0), unpacking with ** in a dictionary display and in a call (PEP 448), keyword arguments collected in the order given (PEP 468), the merge operator | and the update operator |= (PEP 584, Python 3.9), reversed() since Python 3.8, and collections.Counter, defaultdict, OrderedDict and ChainMap for counting, grouping and layering; the chapter's characterCount program is the pattern that Counter and defaultdict(int) replace.

For structuring data, the chapter's dictionaries of dictionaries are today accompanied by the TypedDict (PEP 589), which names the keys and their types for a type checker but is an ordinary dict at run time, by the dataclass, by types.MappingProxyType for a read-only view, by the mapping patterns of the match statement (PEP 634) that take a dictionary apart by its keys, by the json module that writes a nested dictionary as text and refuses keys that are not of a basic type, and by copy.deepcopy where the nested dictionaries of a copy must not be shared with the original.
title: Dictionaries for an advanced course: chapter 7 of the 3rd edition and today's Python

nodes.label: Dictionary basics
nodes.body: The dictionary type, the keys that index it and the way two dictionaries compare are the base of Chapter 7 (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Structure
nodes.body: The chapter starts from the dictionary value written between curly brackets and from the ways Python offers to build one (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Dictionary type
nodes.body: my_cat = {'size': 'fat', 'color': 'gray', 'age': 17} has the keys 'size', 'color' and 'age', and my_cat['size'] is 'fat' and 'My cat has ' + my_cat['color'] + ' fur.' is 'My cat has gray fur.' (Sweigart, 2025); the empty dictionary is {} and is of type dict, while {'a'} is a set because an empty pair of braces cannot also be an empty set, as executed for this study (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A dictionary is a mutable collection of key-value pairs written between curly brackets; a key picks its value the way an index picks an item of a list, but a key may be of almost any type and each key occurs only once; {} is the empty dictionary, and an empty set has no literal.

nodes.label: Dictionary constructors
nodes.body: The chapter enters every dictionary as a literal; the dict constructor also accepts keyword arguments, pairs, another mapping and zip of two lists, so that dict(one=1, two=2, three=3), dict(zip(['one', 'two', 'three'], [1, 2, 3])) and dict([('two', 2), ('one', 1), ('three', 3)]) are all equal to {'one': 1, 'two': 2, 'three': 3}, keyword arguments work only for keys that are valid names, and dict([('k', 1), ('k', 2)]) is {'k': 2} because the last value for a repeated key wins; the chapter as read does not present the constructor (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The dict constructor builds a dictionary from keyword arguments, from pairs, from another mapping or from zip of two lists, and when a key occurs twice the last value wins; keyword arguments work only for keys that are valid names.

nodes.label: Keys
nodes.body: A dictionary is read through its keys, which must be hashable and which may be of many types (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Keys not indexes
nodes.body: With spam = {12345: 'Luggage Combination', 42: 'The Answer'}, spam[12345] is 'Luggage Combination' and spam[42] is 'The Answer', while spam[0] raises KeyError: 0, because the dictionary has keys and no index 0 through 41, and a missing 'color' key raises KeyError: 'color' whose message is the repr of the key (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A dictionary has keys, not positions: d[0] looks for a key equal to 0, and raises KeyError when there is none, even though the dictionary holds two items; a missing key is reported as KeyError with the key as its message.

io.code: (lambda d: (d[42], 0 in d, len(d)))({12345: 'Luggage Combination', 42: 'The Answer'})

nodes.label: Hashable keys
nodes.body: The chapter says that a list or a dictionary cannot be a key because these types are unhashable, and that a tuple should be used where a list is wanted (Sweigart, 2025); under 3.14.4 {[1, 2]: 'x'} raises TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'list') and the same for a dictionary, a tuple such as (2, 3) works as a key, a tuple holding a list as in (1, [2]) is refused with TypeError: cannot use 'tuple' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'list'), and a class that defines __eq__ and no __hash__ is unhashable too, the rule being that a key's hash must not change while it is in the dictionary (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A key must be hashable, so a number, a string or a tuple of hashable items can be a key while a list or a dictionary cannot; the chapter calls these types unhashable and suggests a tuple where a list is wanted, and a tuple that holds a list is refused too.

nodes.label: Equal keys share a slot
nodes.body: {1: 'a', 1.0: 'b', True: 'c'} is {1: 'c'}, because 1, 1.0 and True are equal and have the same hash, so the later assignments replace the value and the first key object, an int, stays; the chapter as read does not present this (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Keys that compare equal and have the same hash are one key, so 1, 1.0 and True name a single pair, which keeps the first key object and takes the last value.

nodes.label: Comparison
nodes.body: The chapter compares dictionaries with lists by equality and by order (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Order insensitive equality
nodes.body: ['cats', 'dogs', 'moose'] == ['dogs', 'moose', 'cats'] is False but eggs == ham is True for {'name': 'Zophie', 'species': 'cat', 'age': '8'} and the same pairs entered in another order, although list(eggs) and list(ham) differ, so equality of dictionaries ignores the order while the order of the keys in each is kept (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Two dictionaries are equal when they hold the same pairs, whatever the order in which the pairs were entered, where two lists are equal only when their items are in the same order.

nodes.label: Insertion order
nodes.body: The chapter says that items in dictionaries are unordered and that there is no first item (Sweigart, 2025); under Python 3.14.4 list({'one': 1, 'two': 2, 'three': 3, 'four': 4}) is ['one', 'two', 'three', 'four'], after d['one'] = 42, del d['two'] and d['two'] = None the dictionary is {'one': 42, 'three': 3, 'four': 4, 'two': None}, so a replaced value keeps its place and a re-added key goes last, and the documentation guarantees this order since Python 3.7 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Since Python 3.7 a dictionary remembers the order in which its keys were first inserted and every loop, list and display follows that order; replacing a value keeps the position of its key and a key added after a deletion goes to the end; the chapter's statement that items are unordered describes older versions.

nodes.label: Mapping not sequence
nodes.body: The chapter says that, because a dictionary is not ordered, it is not a sequence and cannot be sliced (Sweigart, 2025); under 3.14.4 d[0:2] raises KeyError: slice(0, 2, None), since a slice is a hashable key since Python 3.12, {'a': 1} < {'a': 2} raises TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'dict' and 'dict', isinstance(d, Mapping) is True and isinstance(d, Sequence) is False, and list(reversed(d)) is ['two', 'four', 'three', 'one'] for the dictionary above, reversed order of insertion since Python 3.8 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A dictionary is a mapping and not a sequence: it cannot be sliced, the subscript d[0:2] is looked up as a key, and only equality, not ordering, can be used to compare two dictionaries.

nodes.label: Reading and changing
nodes.body: Reading a value, testing for a key and changing the pairs of a dictionary are the operations the chapter builds on the dictionary type (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Reading
nodes.body: A key is tested with in, read with a subscript or with get(), and ensured with setdefault() (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Membership on keys
nodes.body: 'color' in spam and 'color' in spam.keys() are both True for {'color': 'red', 'age': 42}, 'age' not in spam.keys() is False, 'red' in spam.values() is True and 'red' in spam alone is False, because the operators on the dictionary itself test keys (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The in and not in operators on a dictionary test for a key, exactly as 'color' in spam.keys() does; a value is tested with spam.values().

io.code: (lambda d: ('color' in d, 'color' in d.keys(), 'red' in d.values(), 'red' in d))({'color': 'red', 'age': 42})

nodes.label: Get method
nodes.body: picnic_items.get('cups', 0) is 2 and picnic_items.get('eggs', 0) is 0 for {'apples': 5, 'cups': 2}, so the chapter's sentences I am bringing 2 cups. and I am bringing 0 eggs. come out, and picnic_items['eggs'] raises KeyError: 'eggs' (Sweigart, 2025); get without a fallback gives None and never adds the key to the dictionary (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The get method takes a key and a fallback and returns the value of the key or the fallback without adding anything to the dictionary; without a fallback it gives None, so it never raises KeyError.

nodes.label: Setdefault method
nodes.body: spam.setdefault('color', 'black') on {'name': 'Pooka', 'age': 5} returns 'black' and leaves {'name': 'Pooka', 'age': 5, 'color': 'black'}, and spam.setdefault('color', 'white') returns 'black' and changes nothing (Sweigart, 2025); groups.setdefault('even', []).append(2) followed by the same with 4 and with 'odd' and 1 gives {'even': [2, 4], 'odd': [1]} (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The setdefault method stores a value only when the key is absent and returns the value the key has afterwards, so it replaces a three-line if test and leaves an existing value alone.

nodes.label: Changing
nodes.body: A dictionary changes in the same object by assignment to a key, by del, by pop and popitem, by update and by the merge operators (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Add or replace pair
nodes.body: The birthdays program stores a new birthday with birthdays[name] = bday, which adds the key 'Eve' with 'Dec 5' and would replace the value of an existing name, and the chapter notes that everything entered is forgotten when the program ends (Sweigart, 2025); assigning to an existing key keeps its place in the order (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Assigning to a key adds the pair when the key is new and replaces the value when it exists; the chapter's birthday program uses it to grow its dictionary while it runs, and everything entered is lost when the program ends.

nodes.label: Delete pair
nodes.body: The chessboard program's remove command is del main_board[response[1]], which deletes the pair of a square so that the piece disappears; under 3.14.4 del d['a'] on {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3, 'd': 4} leaves {'b': 2, 'c': 3, 'd': 4}, del d['zz'] raises KeyError: 'zz', and clear() leaves {} (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The del statement removes the pair of a key and returns nothing, and raises KeyError when the key is absent; clear empties the whole dictionary.

nodes.label: Pop method
nodes.body: pop() is not in the chapter as read; under 3.14.4 d.pop('b') returns 2 and removes the pair, d.pop('zz', 'absent') returns 'absent', d.pop('zz') raises KeyError: 'zz', and d.popitem() returns the last pair inserted, ('d', 4), and on an empty dictionary raises KeyError: 'popitem(): dictionary is empty', the last-in first-out order being guaranteed since Python 3.7 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The pop method removes a key and returns its value, returns the fallback when one is given and the key is absent, and raises KeyError when there is no fallback; popitem removes and returns the most recently inserted pair.

nodes.label: Update and merge
nodes.body: update() is not in the chapter as read; under 3.14.4 d.update({'b': 20, 'c': 3}, d=4) returns None and gives {'a': 1, 'b': 20, 'c': 3, 'd': 4}, a | b gives {'x': 1, 'y': 20, 'z': 3} from {'x': 1, 'y': 2} and {'y': 20, 'z': 3} and leaves a at {'x': 1, 'y': 2}, a |= b changes a itself, d |= [('b', 2)] accepts pairs while {'a': 1} | [('b', 2)] raises TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'dict' and 'list', and {**{'x': 1, 'y': 2}, **{'y': 20}} is {'x': 1, 'y': 20} (Python Software Foundation, 2026) (D'Aprano and Bucher, 2019) (Landau, 2013).
nodes.definition: The update method copies the pairs of another mapping or of keyword arguments into a dictionary and returns None; since Python 3.9 the | operator gives a new merged dictionary and |= updates in place, and in both the right-hand values win.

nodes.label: Fromkeys method
nodes.body: dict.fromkeys('abc', 0) is {'a': 0, 'b': 0, 'c': 0}, but dict.fromkeys('ab', []) gives both keys the same list, so appending 1 through one key shows it under both as {'a': [1], 'b': [1]}, while {k: [] for k in 'ab'} gives each key its own list; the method is not in the chapter as read (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The class method fromkeys builds a dictionary from an iterable of keys that all share one value, which is safe for a number and a trap for a list, since every key then holds the same list.

nodes.label: First program
nodes.body: The chapter's first program keeps a dictionary of birthdays between questions (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Birthday lookup
nodes.body: birthdays.py holds {'Alice': 'Apr 1', 'Bob': 'Dec 12', 'Carol': 'Mar 4'}, tests a typed name with in, prints birthdays[name] or asks for a birthday and stores it, and with the answers Alice, Eve, Dec 5, Eve and a blank line the program printed exactly the chapter's exchange, ending with Dec 5 is the birthday of Eve and a last prompt (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The chapter's first program keeps names and birthdays in a dictionary, looks a name up with in, answers from the dictionary and asks for a birthday to add when the name is new, looping until a blank name.

io.code: (lambda b, n: b[n] + ' is the birthday of ' + n if n in b else 'I do not have birthday information for ' + n)({'Alice': 'Apr 1', 'Bob': 'Dec 12', 'Carol': 'Mar 4'}, 'Alice')

children.label: 'I do not have birthday information for '

nodes.label: Views and loops
nodes.body: The views of a dictionary and the loops over it are the chapter's second topic, together with the comprehension that builds one (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Views
nodes.body: The methods keys(), values() and items() return view objects (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Keys values items
nodes.body: For {'color': 'red', 'age': 42}, spam.keys() prints dict_keys(['color', 'age']), spam.values() prints dict_values(['red', 42]), spam.items() prints dict_items([('color', 'red'), ('age', 42)]) and the items are tuples, list(spam.keys()) is ['color', 'age'], and spam.keys().append('x') raises AttributeError: 'dict_keys' object has no attribute 'append' while spam.keys()[0] raises TypeError: 'dict_keys' object is not subscriptable (Sweigart, 2025); the chapter calls the views list-like values that cannot be modified (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The methods keys, values and items return dict_keys, dict_values and dict_items views that can be looped over and tested with in but are not lists, cannot be changed and have no append; list() turns a view into a list, and the items are tuples of key and value.

nodes.label: Live and set like views
nodes.body: A view follows the dictionary: after keys = dishes.keys() and the deletion of two entries, list(keys) is ['bacon', 'spam'] and list(values) is [1, 500], values.mapping is a read-only view of the dictionary, keys & {'eggs', 'bacon', 'salad'} is {'bacon'}, {'a': 1}.items() <= {'a': 1, 'b': 2}.items() is True, and d.values() == d.values() is False because values views are never equal; the chapter as read does not present this (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A view is a live window on its dictionary, so it shows later changes, and a keys view or an items view supports the set operators such as & and <= against any iterable.

nodes.label: Looping
nodes.body: A for loop over a dictionary takes the keys, the values or the pairs, in insertion order (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Items loop
nodes.body: for k, v in spam.items() assigns the key and the value of each pair to two names, printing Key: color Value: red and Key: age Value: 42, because each item of the view is a tuple and the loop uses multiple assignment (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A for loop over items() with two names takes the key and the value of every pair in turn, using the same multiple assignment as for a list of pairs.

nodes.label: Sorted and reversed loops
nodes.body: For d = {'b': 1, 'c': 3, 'a': 2}, sorted(d) is ['a', 'b', 'c'], list(reversed(d)) is ['a', 'c', 'b'], sorted(d.items(), key=lambda p: p[1]) is [('b', 1), ('a', 2), ('c', 3)] and sorted(d, key=d.get, reverse=True) is ['c', 'a', 'b']; the chapter as read does not present sorting a dictionary (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A loop visits the keys in insertion order; sorted(d) gives the keys in sorted order, reversed(d) in reverse insertion order (since Python 3.8), and sorted(d.items(), key=...) orders pairs by a chosen part.

io.code: (lambda d: (sorted(d), list(reversed(d)), sorted(d.items(), key=lambda p: p[1])))({'b': 1, 'c': 3, 'a': 2})

nodes.label: Change while looping
nodes.body: Adding keys inside for k in d: d[k + 'x'] = 0 raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration, deleting over list(d) leaves {'c': 3} from {'b': 1, 'c': 3, 'a': 2} when values below 3 are removed, and assigning new values to existing keys during the loop is allowed, turning the values into 10, 30 and 20; the chapter as read does not present the trap (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Adding or deleting keys while looping over a dictionary raises RuntimeError, because the size changed; looping over list(d) or building a new dictionary avoids it, while replacing the value of an existing key is allowed.

io.code: (lambda d: ([d.pop(k) for k in list(d) if d[k] < 2], d)[1])({'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 0})

nodes.label: Building
nodes.body: A dictionary can be built by a loop, by the constructor or by a comprehension (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Dict comprehension
nodes.body: {x: x**2 for x in (2, 4, 6)} is {2: 4, 4: 16, 6: 36}, {v: k for k, v in prices.items()} inverts {'apple': 3, 'pear': 5, 'fig': 9} into {3: 'apple', 5: 'pear', 9: 'fig'}, and an if clause keeps {'pear': 5, 'fig': 9}; the chapter as read does not present dictionary comprehensions (Python Software Foundation, 2026) (Warsaw, 2001).
nodes.definition: A dictionary comprehension builds a dictionary from a key expression, a value expression, a for clause and optional if clauses, so inverting or filtering a dictionary needs no loop with assignments.

nodes.label: Counting and grouping
nodes.body: Counting occurrences and grouping values under keys are the jobs the chapter's setdefault method is shown for, and the standard library has tools for both (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Counting
nodes.body: A dictionary of counts maps each item to the number of times it occurred (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Character count
nodes.body: characterCount.py counts the characters of 'It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.' with count.setdefault(character, 0) and count[character] = count[character] + 1, and under 3.14.4 it printed the dictionary the chapter prints, equal to it and with its keys in the same order, with 'c' three times, the space 13 times and 'A' once (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The chapter's characterCount program counts the characters of a string by making sure each has a key with setdefault and then adding one, so it works for a string of any length.

io.code: (lambda m, c: ([c.__setitem__(ch, c.setdefault(ch, 0) + 1) for ch in m], c)[1])('mississippi', {})

nodes.label: Counter class
nodes.body: Counter(message) gave a dictionary equal to the hand-made count of characterCount, Counter is a subclass of dict, Counter(message).most_common(3) is [(' ', 13), ('t', 6), ('i', 6)], and Counter('abc')['z'] is 0 without adding 'z'; the chapter as read does not present Counter (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: collections.Counter is a dictionary subclass that counts the items of an iterable in one call, answers 0 for a missing key instead of raising, and lists the commonest items with most_common.

nodes.label: Defaultdict counting
nodes.body: defaultdict(int) with d[ch] += 1 for each character of the message gave a dictionary equal to the same count, because a missing key is filled with int(), which is 0; the chapter as read does not present defaultdict (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A defaultdict is a dictionary with a factory that makes the value of a missing key, so defaultdict(int) starts every count at 0 and d[key] += 1 needs no setdefault.

nodes.label: Grouping
nodes.body: Grouping keeps a list of values for each key (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Grouping into lists
nodes.body: For the pairs [('yellow', 1), ('blue', 2), ('yellow', 3), ('blue', 4), ('red', 1)], g = defaultdict(list) with g[k].append(v) gives sorted(g.items()) equal to [('blue', [2, 4]), ('red', [1]), ('yellow', [1, 3])], and d.setdefault(k, []).append(v) on a plain dictionary groups the same way (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Grouping values by key keeps a list per key, made either with setdefault(key, []) or with defaultdict(list), and the result holds every value under its key in the order met.

io.code: (lambda s: (lambda d: ([d.setdefault(k, []).append(v) for k, v in s], d)[1])({}))([('yellow', 1), ('blue', 2), ('yellow', 3)])

nodes.label: Missing key hook
nodes.body: dd = defaultdict(list) gives dd['x'] as [] and then 'x' in dd is True, but dd.get('y') is None and 'y' in dd is False, because only a subscript calls __missing__, and defaultdict() with no factory raises KeyError: 'k' like a plain dictionary (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A defaultdict fills in a missing key only when it is subscripted, because that calls the method __missing__; get and in do not, so dd.get('y') is None and 'y' in dd is False while dd['x'] creates the key.

nodes.label: Ordered dict type
nodes.body: OrderedDict([('a', 1), ('b', 2)]) == OrderedDict([('b', 2), ('a', 1)]) is False where the same two plain dictionaries are equal, an OrderedDict equals a plain dictionary whatever the order, move_to_end('a') put 'a' last giving ['b', 'a'], and ChainMap(overrides, defaults) looked up 'user' as 'admin' and 'color' as 'red'; the chapter as read does not present them (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: collections.OrderedDict is a dictionary whose equality also compares the order of the keys and that can move a key to the end, which a plain dictionary since Python 3.7 cannot do in one call.

nodes.label: Structuring data
nodes.body: Modelling a real-world thing with nested dictionaries and lists is the chapter's second half (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Modelling
nodes.body: The interactive chessboard shows how a data structure is chosen first and the functions written to fit it (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Chessboard model
nodes.body: The board is a dictionary with keys 'a1' to 'h8' and two-character values such as 'wK' and 'bQ', the absence of a key meaning an empty square, and {'h1': 'bK', 'c6': 'wQ', 'g2': 'bB', 'h5': 'bQ', 'e3': 'wK'} has 5 pieces, no piece on 'd4' and one on 'e3'; STARTING_PIECES as typed holds 32 pieces, 16 white and 16 black (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The chapter models a chessboard as a dictionary whose keys are square names such as 'e3' and whose values are two-character piece names such as 'wK'; an empty square is a missing key, and one key per square means one piece per square.

nodes.label: Chessboard printer
nodes.body: print_chessboard(board) loops y over '87654321' and x over 'abcdefgh', so the squares come in the order a8, b8 and on to h8 and then a7, which is left to right although the chapter's text says right to left, appends the piece or the white or black empty-square string, flips is_white_square after each square and again after each row, and prints a template with 64 pairs of braces over 27 lines, which for the five-piece board printed the text board with wQ on c6, bQ on h5, wK on e3, bB on g2 and bK on h1 (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The function print_chessboard visits the 64 squares from a8 to h1 with two nested loops, collects a piece string or a white or black empty-square string for each, and prints the multiline template with format(*squares).

io.code: [x + y for y in '87' for x in 'abc']

nodes.label: Star syntax
nodes.body: BOARD_TEMPLATE.format(*squares) passes the 64 strings of the list as 64 arguments, print(*['cat', 'dog', 'rat']) prints cat dog rat, '{}-{}-{}'.format(*['cat', 'dog', 'rat']) is 'cat-dog-rat', and '{} {} {}'.format(['cat', 'dog', 'rat']) without the star raises IndexError: Replacement index 1 out of range for positional args tuple (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A star before a list in a call passes its items as separate arguments, so print(*spam) means print('cat', 'dog', 'rat'), and the template's 64 pairs of braces take the 64 strings of the list.

nodes.label: Chessboard commands
nodes.body: The simulator splits the typed line, 'move e2 e4'.split() being ['move', 'e2', 'e4'], and acts by dictionary operations: move assigns the piece to the new key and deletes the old, remove deletes, set assigns, reset copies STARTING_PIECES, clear rebinds an empty dictionary, fill assigns a piece to all 64 keys and quit calls sys.exit(); with the command handling run on lines instead of input(), move e2 e4 left 32 pieces with e4 holding wP, fill wP gave 64 squares of 'wP', reset gave a board equal to but not the same object as STARTING_PIECES, and move e3 e4 and remove e3 on the starting board raised KeyError: 'e3', move e2 raised IndexError: list index out of range, and move e2 e7 captured the pawn on e7 and left 31 pieces, since the program checks nothing (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The interactive simulator splits each typed line into a list and uses its first word to choose among move, remove, set, reset, clear, fill and quit, each of which is one or two dictionary operations; it checks nothing, so a command about an empty square raises KeyError.

nodes.label: Nesting
nodes.body: A dictionary value may itself be a dictionary or a list (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Nested dictionaries
nodes.body: all_guests = {'Alice': {'apples': 5, 'pretzels': 12}, 'Bob': {'ham sandwiches': 3, 'apples': 2}, 'Carol': {'cups': 3, 'apple pies': 1}} holds a dictionary of items for each guest, and all_guests['Alice']['apples'] is 5 by two subscripts while all_guests['Bob'].get('cups', 0) is 0 (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A dictionary value can itself be a dictionary or a list, so a dictionary of dictionaries models a picnic in which each guest has their own items, and two subscripts reach an inner value.

nodes.label: Total brought
nodes.body: total_brought(guests, item) loops over guests.items(), adds v.get(item, 0) for each guest and printed Number of things being brought: with Apples 7, Cups 3, Cakes 0, Ham Sandwiches 3 and Apple Pies 1, as the chapter prints (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The function total_brought loops over the guests' inner dictionaries and adds the quantity of an item with get(item, 0), so a guest who brings none of it adds nothing and no KeyError arises.

io.code: (lambda g: sum(v.get('apples', 0) for v in g.values()))({'Alice': {'apples': 5, 'pretzels': 12}, 'Bob': {'ham sandwiches': 3, 'apples': 2}, 'Carol': {'cups': 3, 'apple pies': 1}})

nodes.label: Copying dictionaries
nodes.body: copy.copy(STARTING_PIECES) gives the board a copy it can change, so moving e2 to e4 on the copy left the starting dictionary at its two pieces, and STARTING.copy() == STARTING with STARTING.copy() is STARTING False and dict(STARTING) another new dictionary; for a nested dictionary d.copy() shares the inner dictionary, so after nested['a']['x'] = 9 the shallow copy shows {'a': {'x': 9}} and copy.deepcopy shows {'a': {'x': 1}} (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: copy.copy, d.copy() and dict(d) make a shallow copy: a flat dictionary such as the starting position is then independent of its copy, but a nested one still shares its inner dictionaries, for which copy.deepcopy is needed.

io.code: (lambda c, d: (lambda s, dp: (d['a'].__setitem__('x', 9), s['a']['x'], dp['a']['x'])[1:])(d.copy(), c.deepcopy(d)))(__import__('copy'), {'a': {'x': 1}})

nodes.label: Notation
nodes.body: Nested data can be shown, typed, written out and taken apart with the standard library, beyond the chapter (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Pretty printing
nodes.body: Question 8 asks for the module and function that pretty-print a dictionary, which is pprint and pprint.pprint; with width=40 pprint.pprint printed a nested dictionary over several lines with the keys in sorted order and pprint.pp in insertion order, pformat({'b': 1, 'a': 2}) returns the text {'a': 2, 'b': 1} and with sort_dicts=False the text {'b': 1, 'a': 2}, and json.dumps with sort_keys=True writes the nested dictionary as text, json.loads reads it back and a tuple key raises TypeError: keys must be str, int, float, bool or None, not tuple; the chapter as read does not teach pprint or json (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The pprint module prints a nested structure over several lines when it is too wide; pprint.pprint sorts the keys of a dictionary by default and pprint.pp keeps their insertion order, and pformat returns the text instead of printing it.

nodes.label: Typed models
nodes.body: A class Piece(TypedDict) with color and kind fields gave Piece(color='w', kind='K') equal to the plain dictionary {'color': 'w', 'kind': 'K'} of type dict, with its types in Piece.__annotations__, so nothing is checked at run time; a dataclass Square('e', 4) prints Square(file='e', rank=4), and MappingProxyType({'a': 1}) gives a view that can be read but not assigned to, raising TypeError: 'mappingproxy' object does not support item assignment; the chapter as read does not present them (Python Software Foundation, 2026) (Lehtosalo, 2019).
nodes.definition: A TypedDict names the keys a dictionary should have and their types for a type checker, but at run time it is an ordinary dict; a dataclass or a named tuple is the alternative when the record should be an object with attributes.

nodes.label: Mapping pattern
nodes.body: In a match statement the pattern {'op': 'move', 'from': a, 'to': b} matched {'op': 'move', 'from': 'e2', 'to': 'e4', 'extra': 1} and bound the two squares, {'op': str(o), **rest} collected the remaining keys, giving unknown fill with ['piece'], and a list matched none of them; the chapter as read does not present the match statement (Python Software Foundation, 2026) (Bucher and van Rossum, 2020).
nodes.definition: A match statement can test the keys of a dictionary with a mapping pattern, which succeeds when the listed keys are present, binds names to their values, ignores extra keys and can collect them with **rest.

io.code: (lambda ns: (exec(chr(10).join(['def f(v):', '    match v:', '        case {1: a, **rest}:', '            return a, sorted(rest)', '        case _:', '            return None']), ns), ns['f']({1: 'e2', 2: 'e4', 3: 0}), ns['f']([1]))[1:])({})

nodes.label: Practice work
nodes.body: The chapter closes with 8 practice questions and 3 practice programs (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Questions
nodes.body: The practice questions are answered by the dictionary operations of the chapter (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Practice questions
nodes.body: Run for this study, question 1 is {}, question 2 is {'foo': 42}, question 4 raises KeyError: 'foo' for spam['foo'] with spam = {'bar': 100}, in spam and in spam.keys() are both True for a key and only in spam.values() tests values, the shortcut of question 7 is spam.setdefault('color', 'black') which gave the same dictionary as the if test, and question 8, pprint.pformat({'b': 2, 'a': 1}), returns the text {'a': 1, 'b': 2} (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The eight practice questions ask for an empty dictionary, a one-pair dictionary, the difference between a dictionary and a list, the KeyError of a missing key, in against keys() and values(), the setdefault shortcut and pprint for printing a dictionary.

nodes.label: Programs
nodes.body: The three practice programs apply the dictionary to a chessboard check, a game inventory and a list of loot (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Chess validator
nodes.body: A validator written for this study for the chapter's own notation accepted the 32-piece starting position and the five-piece board, and refused a board with the square 'z9', one with no white king, one with the piece 'wX' and one with 9 white pawns; the practice program itself speaks of squares from '1a' to '8h' and of pieces named 'pawn' or 'knight', which differs from the chapter's 'a1' and 'wP' (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The first practice program asks for a function that tells whether a chessboard dictionary is valid: exactly one king of each colour, at most 16 pieces and 8 pawns each, and every piece on a real square; the chapter's wording of the square and piece names differs from its own notation.

io.code: (lambda b: (sum(v == 'bK' for v in b.values()), sum(v == 'wK' for v in b.values())))({'h1': 'bK', 'c6': 'wQ', 'g2': 'bB', 'h5': 'bQ', 'e3': 'wK'})

nodes.label: Fantasy inventory
nodes.body: display_inventory(stuff) for {'rope': 1, 'torch': 6, 'gold coin': 42, 'dagger': 1, 'arrow': 12} printed Inventory:, the lines 1 rope, 6 torch, 42 gold coin, 1 dagger and 12 arrow in insertion order, and Total number of items: 62, where the chapter's sample lists 12 arrow first, an order a loop over items() does not give (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The second practice program models a game inventory as a dictionary from item name to count and prints each pair followed by the total number of items, summing the values while looping over items().

nodes.label: Loot conversion
nodes.body: add_to_inventory(inv, dragon_loot) with inventory.get(item, 0) + 1 for each item turned {'gold coin': 42, 'rope': 1} and ['gold coin', 'dagger', 'gold coin', 'gold coin', 'ruby'] into gold coin 45, rope 1, dagger 1 and ruby 1, a total of 48, where the chapter's sample lists ruby before dagger and a blank line before the total (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The third practice program turns a list that may repeat items into counts in a dictionary, adding one to the current count of each item, which get(item, 0) makes safe for a new item.

io.code: (lambda inv, loot: [inv.__setitem__(i, inv.get(i, 0) + 1) for i in loot] and inv)({'gold coin': 42, 'rope': 1}, ['gold coin', 'dagger', 'gold coin', 'gold coin', 'ruby'])

resources.title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition: Chapter 7, Dictionaries and Structuring Data
resources.why: The course textbook's own chapter, free online: dictionaries, the birthdays and characterCount programs, the chessboard and the picnic.

resources.title: Built-in Types (mapping types and dictionary views)
resources.why: Every dictionary method and operator, insertion order, the views, and what __missing__ is.

resources.title: 5. Data Structures (dictionaries and looping techniques)
resources.why: The tutorial's account of dictionaries, dict comprehensions and looping over items().

resources.title: collections - Container datatypes
resources.why: Counter, defaultdict, OrderedDict and ChainMap, with worked examples of counting and grouping.

resources.title: pprint - Data pretty printer
resources.why: The answer to practice question 8, and the difference between pprint.pprint and pprint.pp.

resources.title: copy - Shallow and deep copy operations
resources.why: Why copying a nested dictionary needs deepcopy.

resources.title: 3. Data model (object.__hash__)
resources.why: The rule behind unhashable keys: what a hash must do and when a class is unhashable.

resources.title: typing - Support for type hints (TypedDict)
resources.why: TypedDict: a dictionary whose keys and value types a checker knows, and a plain dict at run time.

resources.title: json - JSON encoder and decoder
resources.why: How a nested dictionary becomes text and which keys json accepts.

resources.title: PEP 584 - Add Union Operators To dict
resources.why: Why dict got | and |=, and what they do with shared keys.

resources.title: PEP 274 - Dict Comprehensions
resources.why: The dictionary comprehension and how it came to Python 2.7 and 3.0.

resources.title: PEP 634 - Structural Pattern Matching: Specification
resources.why: The mapping pattern: how a match statement takes a dictionary apart by its keys.

resources.title: PEP 589 - TypedDict: Type Hints for Dictionaries with a Fixed Set of Keys
resources.why: The design of TypedDict for records with a fixed set of string keys.
